bull_thesis: OKEA is a small Norwegian oil and gas producer that buys mature fields on the Norwegian continental shelf from the majors and extends their lives. Second, the project delivering most of that is physically de-risked rather than promised: the Bestla field tied back to the Brage platform has had its flowlines laid and its topside connections completed, with the wellhead assembly scheduled for September 2026 and start-up still targeted for early 2027 - the same date management gave a full year earlier, in July 2025. A date that survives twelve months of scrutiny in offshore construction is worth more than a new one. Third, the balance sheet has genuinely turned: net debt of about 77 million dollars at the end of 2025 became roughly 31 million dollars of net cash by 30 June 2026 (59 million dollars on the company's own definition, which excludes leases), and that improvement was achieved while spending 195 million dollars on capital projects in the same six months. bear_thesis: The bear case starts with the observation that most of the cheapness in this file is a data artefact, and the rest has already been collected by someone else. Three corrections matter. The trailing free cash flow of 162 million dollars in the input is wrong by roughly four times: the data feed dropped the first quarter of 2026's 117.9 million dollars of capital spend, and rebuilding the four quarters by hand from operating cash flow minus capital spend gives about 44 million dollars. consensus_delta: For a company screened as deep value, the right question is whether the market is pricing terminal decline into stable earning power. Three street assumptions look wrong to us. First, and most consequential, is the claim circulating in Norwegian retail research that 2027 delivers a swing of roughly 300 million dollars in free cash flow because capital spending collapses. It does not, and the reason is arithmetic rather than opinion: Norway taxes offshore profit at 78% at the margin and allows capital spending to be deducted against that same rate largely in the year it is incurred, so the state is already funding about 78% of the programme. Guidance has capital spending falling from 300-360 million dollars in 2026 to 230-290 million in 2027 - about 70 million dollars at the midpoint - and the shareholder keeps roughly 22 cents of each of those dollars, so perhaps 15 million dollars, not 70. Second, the sell side's published targets of roughly 44 to 47 kroner, with a high of 52 and a low of 40 across five analysts, are close to our own base case of 48 - which is itself the point. forcing_function: Four dated or near-dated events could force a re-rating, in ascending order of importance. positioning_washout: There is no mechanical forced-selling dynamic to exploit here, and pretending otherwise would be the error. moderator_conclusion: Wait for the wash-out, at a named level. This is a competently run business that has been wrongly described by our own data, and correcting the description removes most of the reason to buy it today. Three of the screener's headline signals are artefacts: the 93% revenue collapse is a change of reporting currency from kroner to dollars, the trailing free cash flow of 162 million dollars omits a full quarter of capital spending and should read about 44 million, and the discounted-cash-flow fair value of 427 follows from those broken inputs. What remains once they are stripped out is a real but ordinary discount, not a deep-value dislocation. Our sum-of-the-parts, built as an after-tax cash annuity across roughly 75 million barrels of net proved-and-probable reserves rather than on any pre-tax multiple, lands at about 48 kroner a share against 36.40 today - a margin of safety near 24%, against an adverse case at 24 kroner that is a similar distance below. Roughly symmetric risk and reward is not a reason to commit capital, particularly with no structural floor beneath the price: the net cash of about 3 kroner a share sits in front of a 1,009 million dollar gross decommissioning obligation and 107 million dollars of book equity. Judged purely on value, ignoring events entirely, this rates a middling score for the same reasons - the discount is modest, and the forensic quality does not support paying up. Shareholders' equity has been reduced to almost nothing by repeated write-downs, including 86 million dollars against the Statfjord interests bought from Equinor in 2023, the solvency score of 1.8 sits inside the distress band, and 2026 production guidance was cut one year after it was set. There is no moat in any defensible sense: this is an undifferentiated commodity sold at a global price, with a 4.2% return on invested capital and a negative return on equity. What the company does have is a genuine and demonstrated capability at extending the life of late-stage fields - 58 million barrels added at Brage, 62 million at Draugen, with economic lives pushed to 2035 and 2040 - and that capability is worth respecting even though it is not a barrier to entry. The energy transition is the obvious structural threat and OKEA is on the wrong side of it, but the damage is manageable rather than terminal here for a structural reason: these are seven-to-twelve-year depleting assets, so almost none of the present value sits beyond 2040 where that risk concentrates, and Norway carries 78% of the abandonment cost through tax relief. Two considerations settle the timing. First, this market environment - a central bank with a hiking bias, a 30-year yield above 5% and the highest long rate since 2007 - raises the discount rate on every story and pays events with a date and a cash payoff. OKEA's events are dated only in management's own words, and its one recent comparable date slipped four months. Second, and more binding, is the standing preference for holdings whose outcomes resolve independently. OKEA resolves on Brent crude, which the current regime read names as one of two dominant shared factors and explicitly warns is a headline derivative rather than something to underwrite - Brent round-tripped from above 100 dollars in late July to 86 today on a de-escalation Iran has not confirmed. An unhedged small producer is the purest possible expression of exactly the single-factor exposure we are trying to avoid concentrating. The catalyst being soft rather than hard is neither a mark for nor against the name in this book, and the fact that the shares have already doubled is not by itself disqualifying - post-event re-rates often keep running. The disqualifier is simply the price: 36.40 kroner is 21% above the 200-day average and 66% of the way up a wide 52-week range, and it does not offer enough room. Two things would change the call. A pullback to around 30 kroner, the 200-day average, would restore a discount in the mid-30s of percent and make this an entry. Alternatively, confirmed Bestla first oil combined with a formal dividend plan that clears the bond covenant thresholds would justify paying up, because it would convert a guided step-up into a delivered one and bring a whole class of Norwegian income buyers back to a stock they currently cannot own.

Four pieces of evidence support it. First, the production step-up is guided and specific: management raised 2027 output guidance to 39,000-43,000 barrels of oil equivalent per day on the 16 July 2026 call, up from 37,000-41,000 and against 29,000-32,000 for 2026 - roughly a third more barrels. Second, the project delivering most of that is physically de-risked rather than promised: the Bestla field tied back to the Brage platform has had its flowlines laid and its topside connections completed, with the wellhead assembly scheduled for September 2026 and start-up still targeted for early 2027 - the same date management gave a full year earlier, in July 2025. Third, the balance sheet has genuinely turned: net debt of about 77 million dollars at the end of 2025 became roughly 31 million dollars of net cash by 30 June 2026 (59 million dollars on the company's own definition, which excludes leases), and that improvement was achieved while spending 195 million dollars on capital projects in the same six months. On top of that, the dividend suspended in early 2024 could return once the company clears the distribution thresholds in its bond covenants, which the chief financial officer described in July 2026 as close and improving.
